patient.chief_complaint: Sudden severe headache 2 hours ago, but now improved to 3/10, worried about something serious
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Jenkins is a 42-year-old male with hypertension who presents with sudden onset severe headache 2 hours ago that has partially resolved. He was exercising at the gym when he experienced an explosive headache that reached 10/10 within seconds. He felt nauseated and sat down. The headache has improved significantly over the past 2 hours to 3/10, and he almost did not come to the ED, but a colleague at the fire station (who is a paramedic) insisted he be evaluated. He is a firefighter and reports his blood pressure can run high. He took ibuprofen (not prescribed, borrowed from colleague) which partially helped. He denies any loss of consciousness, vomiting, focal weakness, or neck stiffness. He has no prior history of severe headaches. He states the headache was during a heavy squat exercise. On arrival, he appears well and is not in significant distress. His blood pressure is mildly elevated. The diagnostic challenge is that he appears well, the headache is significantly improved, and he has a logical explanation (exertional headache during lifting). No nuchal rigidity on initial exam.

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented x4; GCS 15; appears well; mild residual headache 3/10
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: PERRL 3mm; EOM intact; no papilledema; no CN deficit
neurological_exam.additional: No nuchal rigidity on initial exam; no Kernig; patient appears well - the diagnostic puzzle is that clinical presentation is reassuring but history is classic SAH

findings.location: Posterior interhemispheric fissure and prepontine cistern
findings.description: Very subtle hyperdensity in posterior interhemispheric fissure - pattern consistent with perimesencephalic SAH

additional_observations: Easy to miss without careful review
ct.impression: Very subtle subarachnoid hemorrhage in perimesencephalic and posterior interhemispheric regions. Pattern is consistent with perimesencephalic SAH (which is often non-aneurysmal and has benign prognosis), but aneurysmal SAH from basilar apex or posterior fossa aneurysm must be excluded. LP and CTA are required.
recommended_actions: CTA to exclude posterior fossa aneurysm

findings.finding: No saccular, fusiform, or mycotic aneurysm identified

output.impression: CTA head and neck is NEGATIVE for intracranial aneurysm. No AVM identified. In the context of perimesencephalic hemorrhage pattern on CT and negative CTA, this is consistent with perimesencephalic non-aneurysmal SAH - a benign entity with excellent prognosis. DSA recommended to definitively exclude aneurysm given this cannot be excluded by CTA alone.
recommended_actions: Conventional DSA to definitively exclude posterior fossa aneurysm
If DSA negative, diagnosis is perimesencephalic SAH - benign prognosis

findings.finding: Complete 6-vessel angiogram negative for any intracranial aneurysm
No AVM, dural AV fistula, or other vascular malformation
All posterior fossa vessels including basilar, PICAs, SCA, PCAs - normal

output.impression: Conventional DSA (gold standard) is completely negative for intracranial aneurysm or vascular malformation. Combined with perimesencephalic hemorrhage pattern on CT, this is diagnostic of perimesencephalic non-aneurysmal SAH. This entity has an excellent prognosis with <1% rebleed risk and no significant vasospasm risk. No intervention required.
recommended_actions: Repeat MRA at 6 months to confirm

output.query: Perimesencephalic non-aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage prognosis management

results.finding: Perimesencephalic SAH: blood centered anterior to brainstem, negative angiogram - benign entity
Rebleed risk <1% (vs 20-30% in first 24h for aneurysmal SAH)
Vasospasm rates very low compared to aneurysmal SAH
Etiology: likely venous origin (perimesencephalic veins/bridging veins) not arterial aneurysm
Prognosis: excellent; most patients return to normal activities; headache may persist weeks

output.summary: Perimesencephalic non-aneurysmal SAH is a distinct entity with benign prognosis. Key features: blood centered anterior to brainstem/perimesencephalic cisterns, negative CTA and DSA, low rebleed risk (<1%), minimal vasospasm risk, and excellent long-term outcomes. No aneurysm treatment needed. This is the definitive diagnosis after DSA excludes aneurysm.

output.impression: No vasospasm on day 3 TCD. Consistent with perimesencephalic SAH (low vasospasm risk compared to aneurysmal SAH). Daily TCD monitoring still recommended days 3-14 per protocol.
recommended_actions: Low but not zero vasospasm risk in perimesencephalic SAH

output.query: Exertional headache SAH differential diagnosis Valsalva

results.finding: Exertional trigger (Valsalva, lifting, coitus) is classic for SAH
Primary exertional headache can mimic SAH but is diagnosis of exclusion after SAH excluded
Ottawa SAH Rule: headache onset during exertion - requires SAH workup

output.summary: Exertional onset thunderclap headache requires SAH workup before any benign diagnosis is accepted. Primary exertional headache is a diagnosis of exclusion. In this case, CSF and CT confirm SAH (perimesencephalic), so the exertional context is the triggering event for the venous hemorrhage, not a benign primary exertional headache.

critical_actions: LP despite improving symptoms - asymptomatic improvement does not exclude SAH
CTA and DSA to exclude posterior fossa aneurysm
Recognize perimesencephalic pattern as distinct from aneurysmal SAH
Do not send home based on benign appearance and improving headache without workup
contraindicated_actions: Do not diagnose primary exertional headache without excluding SAH
Do not skip LP because patient appears well and headache improved
Do not skip DSA because CTA is negative - CTA can miss small posterior fossa aneurysms
Do not falsely reassure about no risk - rebleed risk is low but not zero even in perimesencephalic SAH
key_reasoning_points: Thunderclap headache with exertional onset requires SAH workup regardless of clinical improvement
Perimesencephalic blood distribution (anterior brainstem cisterns) with negative CTA and DSA is diagnostic of perimesencephalic non-aneurysmal SAH
Perimesencephalic SAH has excellent prognosis (<1% rebleed, minimal vasospasm) in contrast to aneurysmal SAH
Normal ECG and normal troponin are consistent with perimesencephalic SAH (less neurogenic cardiac injury)
DSA is required despite negative CTA - CTA can miss small posterior fossa or basilar perforator aneurysms
The diagnostic puzzle: patient appears well, no nuchal rigidity, headache improved, but LP confirms SAH
